headline: High: TREK’s collaborative, MCP-enabled, browser-capable defaults create data-leakage and cascading-error risks when paired with a non-runnable awesome-nlp list that can still be used as untrusted content.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: TREK can use MCP, browsers, and real-time collaboration, so content from awesome-nlp could be copied into TREK workflows and treated as instructions or prompts. awesome-nlp itself is just a static list, so the bridge is indirect, but TREK’s permissive input surfaces make prompt injection plausible. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF TREK ingests text from awesome-nlp into an MCP tool call or browser-assisted workflow, injection becomes reachable.
IF operators manually copy list content into TREK prompts, the bridge exists.
mitigations: Disable MCP for sessions that ingest external text.
Paste awesome-nlp content into a plain-text review buffer first.
Add a prompt delimiter that strips instructions from copied content.
Require human confirmation before any tool call derived from external text.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags for imported content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: TREK touches sensitive classes including API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and documents, and it has files plus allowlisted egress. awesome-nlp is non-runnable and does not itself expose data, but if its content is loaded into TREK, TREK may transmit context to external services. The pairwise leakage path is indirect yet credible in default collaborative use.
conditions: IF TREK loads external text into browser or MCP contexts, that text can be retained in logs or sent to allowlisted services.
IF sensitive travel data is present in the same TREK session as imported content, leakage scope expands.
mitigations: Avoid placing secrets in the same TREK workspace as imported content.
Review allowlisted egress destinations before use.
Clear or rotate session data after importing external text.
Restrict uploads/ to non-sensitive files only.
requires-engineering: separate secret-bearing sessions from content-ingestion sessions.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-nlp has no write, network, or runtime surfaces, while TREK has collaborative real-time state and file-backed storage. That means there is little direct write-write conflict between the pair, but TREK’s mutable workspace can still be affected if operators use awesome-nlp content as shared input. The overlap is mostly one-way and small.
conditions: IF both agents are placed in the same writable workspace through external orchestration, state collisions become possible.
IF TREK instances are run concurrently against ./data/travel.db, conflicts increase.
mitigations: Run only one TREK instance per workspace.
Keep awesome-nlp read-only.
Avoid sharing ./data/travel.db across sessions.
Use separate folders for imported reference material.
requires-engineering: add file locking around mutable TREK state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: TREK is collaborative and AI-built-in, so it may treat imported content as authoritative unless operators verify it. awesome-nlp is a curated list, but it can still seed incorrect or outdated recommendations that TREK renders into plans or actions. The downstream harm is more than trivial because TREK handles reservations and budgets.
conditions: IF TREK uses imported awesome-nlp entries as planning facts without verification, errors can propagate.
IF those propagated facts affect reservations, budgets, or travel documents, the cascade becomes operational.
mitigations: Verify imported recommendations against primary sources.
Mark awesome-nlp content as untrusted reference material.
Require a second-pass review before committing plans.
Limit AI-generated suggestions to draft mode.
requires-engineering: add source-citation enforcement in TREK.

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles user accounts, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while awesome-nlp is a public open-source list with no stated compliance controls. The pair does not show a residency mismatch, but TREK’s sensitive-data handling plus public-source ingestion creates a compliance gap around retention and secret handling. The other agent is cited only as the public source side.
conditions: IF TREK stores imported content alongside secrets in ./data/logs/trek.log or ./data/travel.db, retention risk increases.
IF regulated personal data is entered into TREK, missing policy controls become relevant.
mitigations: Do not paste secrets into imported-content sessions.
Review log retention settings before use.
Purge test data after evaluation.
Separate public reference material from user records.
requires-engineering: document retention and deletion workflows.
